rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 <U+2013> two-year field experiment (2005, 2006) at Bursa with five drip-irrigated deficit treatments in a randomized complete block design with three replications. Q2: Section 3.5 and Fig. 7 <U+2013> regression of WUE on seasonal mean CWSI was polynomial (R2 = 0.67, RMSE = 0.03) and the authors state the highest WUE is obtained at a CWSI close to 0.6; Table 3 gives WUE and mean CWSI per treatment. Q4: Section 2 and Table 2 <U+2013> irrigation amounts measured by water meter and seasonal ETc determined by neutron-probe soil water balance for each treatment, i.e. the water-use pathway (less applied water, lower ETc) through which the CWSI-guided deficit produces higher WUE is measured; Fig. 4 shows the quadratic WUE<U+2013>ETc relation. Q8: Section 3.1 <U+2013> measured ETc of the fully irrigated treatment exceeded FAO-56 estimates and the authors say they cannot define the sources (variety, season length, sub-surface flows, soil evaporation); Section 3.4 <U+2013> the observed VPD range (about 1<U+2013>4 kPa) was narrower than the 1<U+2013>6 kPa suggested for defining a transferable baseline.
rows.notes: The passage is a near-verbatim restatement of the study's own result. The review's technology label 'app_scheduling' does not literally match: the study uses hand-held infrared thermometry and the empirical Idso CWSI, not a software application; the passage itself, however, concerns CWSI, which the study tests, so Q2 is answered on the passage. Q3: WUE<U+2013>CWSI relation derived by a single regression on one data set; no independent second method. Q5/Q6: single site, single soil, single cultivar, plot scale. Q7: the authors say a stress-based schedule could be adopted when water is scarce or costly, which is an adoption rationale rather than a stated condition for the effect to occur. Q9: only R2 and regression RMSE are given for the WUE<U+2013>CWSI relation; no SD, CI or range for WUE in Table 3.

notes: Full text available and complete. Single claim row.
